issues.legal_issue: A manager of a joint Hindu family may borrow a land-improvement loan in a representative capacity under the statutory recovery scheme.
material_facts: The father, who managed a joint Hindu family, obtained a government loan to construct wells and improve land belonging to the family.
The loan application and surrounding circumstances showed that the borrowing was for improving family land, and family property was offered as security.
issues.conclusion: The father could be treated as a borrower in his capacity as manager of the joint family; the statutory term “borrower” was not restricted to an individual borrowing in a personal capacity.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7 of the Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883, does not require that a borrower be an individual, and section 9 contemplates joint borrowers. The word “borrower” therefore includes a manager borrowing for a joint Hindu family. The Court distinguished Sankaran Nambudripad v. Ramaswami Ayyar and Chinnasami Mudaliar v. Tirumalai Pillai as not addressing this question.

predicates.land_improvement_loan_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a loan advanced for improving land and recovered under a statutory loan scheme.
predicates.family_manager_borrowed: The manager of a joint family obtained the loan in circumstances showing that he acted for the family rather than solely for himself.
predicates.loan_for_family_land: The loan was intended to improve land belonging to the joint family.

issues.definition: When a land-improvement loan is obtained by a family manager for family land, the manager may borrow representatively for the family.

issues.legal_issue: Joint family property is liable for a debt incurred by the family manager for the legal necessity or benefit of the joint family estate.
material_facts: The land sought to be sold was joint family property, as the plaintiffs had themselves described it as such in an earlier pleading.
The father obtained the loan to improve joint family agricultural land and offered other joint family land as security.
Agriculture was one of the family’s occupations, and the loan was intended to increase the productive potential of family land.
issues.conclusion: The loan was a joint family debt incurred for the benefit of the joint family estate, and the joint family property was liable for its repayment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a joint family manager has implied authority to borrow for family purposes, and debts incurred for family legal necessity or the benefit of the estate bind the joint family property. The Court relied on Mulla’s Hindu Law, including paragraphs 240 and 251, and treated a loan to improve family agricultural land as being for legal necessity where agriculture was a family occupation.

rule.if: joint_family_property and family_manager_borrowed and loan_improves_family_land and agriculture_is_family_occupation

predicates.joint_family_property: The property to be reached for repayment belonged to the joint family.
predicates.family_manager_borrowed: The family manager obtained the loan in circumstances showing that he acted for the family rather than solely for himself.
predicates.loan_improves_family_land: The loan was used or intended to improve land belonging to the joint family.
predicates.agriculture_is_family_occupation: Agriculture was one of the occupations carried on by the family.

issues.definition: If a family manager borrows to improve family land and agriculture is a family occupation, the family property may be reached to repay the family debt.

issues.legal_issue: A genuine partition does not discharge liability for an unpaid pre-partition family debt when no provision for that debt was made at partition, and sons remain liable for an untainted debt of their father to the extent of family property received.
material_facts: A registered partition between the father and his sons took place while the loan remained unpaid.
The partition made no provision for the outstanding family debts.
The debt was incurred before partition and was not shown to have been incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
issues.conclusion: The property allotted to the sons remained liable for the pre-partition debt; the sons’ pious obligation to pay their father’s untainted debt continued after partition.
issues.legal_principle: Hindu law requires provision to be made for joint family debts when the family estate is partitioned; absent such provision, the sons remain liable for pre-partition debts. The pious obligation extends to a father’s debts not tainted with illegality or immorality. The Court relied on Sat Narain v. Das, Pannalal v. Mst. Naraini, Vriddhachalam Pillai v. Shaldean Syrian Bank Ltd., Muttayan v. Zamindar of Sivagiri, and Anthonyswamy v. M. R. Chinnaswamy Koundan.

rule.if: pre_partition_debt and partition_made and no_debt_provision_at_partition and not debt_tainted

predicates.pre_partition_debt: The debt was incurred before the family partition.
predicates.partition_made: The family estate was partitioned and property was allotted to the sons.
predicates.no_debt_provision_at_partition: The partition arrangement made no provision for payment of the outstanding debt.
predicates.debt_tainted: The debt was incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.

issues.definition: When an untainted debt predates partition and the partition makes no provision for it, property allotted to the sons remains liable for that debt.

issues.legal_issue: A sale in execution for an untainted pre-partition debt is not invalid merely because it occurs after partition or the sons were not parties to the recovery proceeding.
material_facts: Recovery proceedings for the loan began before the partition, although the sale proclamation for the disputed land was issued later.
The sons knew of the intended sale, and the purchaser was put in possession after the sale was confirmed.
The sons did not establish that the debt was tainted with illegality or immorality.
The sale covered the whole property, which the purchaser intended to buy and did buy.
issues.conclusion: The sale could not be set aside solely because it occurred after partition or because the sons were not parties to the recovery proceeding; the sons could challenge it by establishing that the debt was tainted.
issues.legal_principle: A revenue recovery order for a loan recoverable as arrears of land revenue is equivalent to a decree, and a sale proclamation is execution of that decree. The pious obligation continues after partition, and the whole estate may be sold for an untainted pre-partition debt. The sons’ remedy is to challenge the character of the debt in an appropriate proceeding. The Court relied particularly on S. M. Jakati & Sons v. S. M. Borkar, read with Pannalal v. Mst. Naraini, and applied sections 150 and 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code to the recovery process.

rule.if: sale_challenged_in_suit and revenue_recovery_for_pre_partition_debt and property_sold_in_execution and not debt_tainted

predicates.sale_challenged_in_suit: The sons brought a proceeding seeking to set aside a sale of family property for their father’s debt.
predicates.revenue_recovery_for_pre_partition_debt: The recovery process concerned a debt incurred before partition and recoverable through revenue procedures.
predicates.property_sold_in_execution: The property was sold through an execution or revenue-sale process and the purchaser acquired possession.
predicates.debt_tainted: The debt was incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.

issues.definition: In a suit challenging a sale made to recover a pre-partition debt, the sale is not invalid merely because it followed partition or the sons were not parties if the debt was untainted.
